new_statements.quote: A phonological word is a phonological unit consisting of one or more phonological syllables and marked by one or more stresses which are predictable from the tone pattern of the word. There appear to be four degrees of word-stress which will be designated as heavy ('''), medium (''), light (') and unstressed. The stress rules, which comprise an ordered set, are as follows: [1] A high tone receives heavy stress if followed by a low-tone syllable [2] The first in a series of high-tone syllables within a word receives a medium stress [3] A final closed high-tone syllable receives light stress [4] Other final high-tone syllables are unstressed
new_statements.citation: Deibler, Ellis W. 1976. Semantic relationships of Gahuku verbs. SIL Publications in Linguistics and Related Fields 48. Norman, Okla.: Summer Institute of Linguistics / University of Oklahoma. Appendix B, 'Phonological Word Structure', pp. 154-155.
new_statements.locator: Appendix B, pp. 154-155 (PDF pages 170-171); summary statement also Sect. 2.2, p. 6
new_statements.reading: tone language with a stress statement
new_statements.rule_in_words: Alekano has two register tones (H, L) on every syllable, with a very low functional load. Word stress is not positional: it is entirely derived from the word's tone pattern by an ordered rule set. Heaviest stress falls on a H syllable that is followed by a L syllable; the first of a run of H syllables gets medium stress; a word-final closed (glottal) H syllable gets light stress, other final H syllables are unstressed; in a word ending L-H with an open final syllable the penult gets light stress; L syllables are otherwise unstressed. Deibler's 1992 OPD (p. 3) restates this: greatest stress on H followed by L in the same word, lesser stress on a final H preceded by L, light stress on the first of two same-tone syllables.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Four degrees of word stress (heavy, medium, light, unstressed), all predicted from tone; a word may carry more than one stress (p. 154: 'one or more stresses').
new_statements.exceptions: Phonological-clause stress overrides word stress: a clause-final high-tone syllable receives strong stress only if it is the only H syllable in the word, otherwise it is unstressed (p. 155). Enclitics perturb the tone pattern of noun stems in lexically determined classes (pp. 153-154), which changes the stress placement; tone perturbation not fully analyzed (p. 5 fn. 2). Rules 1-3 here are quoted; rules 5-6 (penult light stress in open-final L-H words; L syllables unstressed) are on p. 155.
new_statements.domain_note: Domain is the phonological word ('There are no restrictions on syllable or stress patterns across word boundaries', p. 155); a separate phonological-clause stress and sentence-final downglide are described (pp. 155, Sect. 6.3). Data from the Wanima village variety (author's field site 1959-1979). Language called 'Gahuku' in this source = Alekano.
new_statements.identity_note: All sources describe the same language: 'Gahuku' is the older name for Alekano (glottocode alek1238, ISO gah); Deibler's data are from the village of Wanima, central in the language area (dictionary 2008, p. 2). Young 1962 also uses 'Gahuku'.

sources.note: p. 6: 'The type of stress within a phonological word is predictable from the tone pattern.' Appendix B pp. 154-155 gives an ordered set of six stress rules: four degrees of word stress (heavy, medium, light, unstressed), all assigned from the H/L tone pattern; plus a separate phonological-clause stress rule (clause-final H syllable strongly stressed only if it is the word's only H syllable).

sources.note: p. 3 'Suprasegmentals (tone, stress, length)': 'There are several degrees of stress conditioned by tone. Greatest stress is on a high tone syllable followed by a low tone in the same word. Lesser stress is on a final high tone preceded by a low tone syllable. In a word containing two syllables with the same tone, the first has light stress. Alekano has two phonemic tones. They are not written in the practical orthography because they have an extremely low functional load.'

sources.citation: Wikipedia, 'Alekano language' (phonology section citing the 1992 OPD).
sources.note: Paraphrase: 'Alekano has low and high tones but with a very low functional load. HL receives strong stress, LH lesser stress.' Consistent with the OPD p. 3.

sources.note: Sect. 3.3 'Supra-segmental phonemes' pp. 98-99: 'the contrastive supra-segmental feature is not so much one of pitch levels or stress intensity as of syllable emphasis... In KANITE and GAHUKU it is a phoneme of tone, which has been described as high tone and which contrasts with syllables which may be described as being either low tone or toneless. Minimal word pairs contrast as to the syllables on which the tone is placed' (Gahuku examples 'musi 'bird' / mu'si 'vomit'); p. 99: 'In GAHUKU words that are toneless (or completely low tone) are rare but do occur.' No separate stress rule for Gahu…
